column6: High
column7: Two independent institutional/scholarly summaries agree; verify birth record if located.

column6: Moderate-high

column8: Review ANRI cited records, Tjokroaminoto family material and Sukarno/associates' testimony.

column6: Moderate for relationship; unresolved for exact dates

column2: Sukarno founded the PNI in 1927 after organizing nationalist study networks in Bandung.
column6: High for foundation year; moderate for organizational sequence
column7: ANRI and Cambridge agree on 1927; party records and police surveillance files are not yet reviewed.
column8: Locate PNI founding documents, Dutch intelligence/police files and contemporary press.

column2: Sukarno was arrested by Dutch colonial authorities in 1929, imprisoned through 1931, rearrested in 1933 and exiled to Flores then Bengkulu.
column6: High for broad sequence
column7: Exact arrest/trial/release and transfer dates need direct legal/administrative records.
column8: Search court files, colonial government decisions, prison/exile correspondence.

column2: During Japanese rule Sukarno cooperated with Japanese-sponsored bodies and mobilization, while using those platforms for nationalist organization; this entailed political responsibility in a coercive occupation economy that included romusha forced labor.
column4: Scholarly and archival syntheses; disputed moral/political interpretation
column6: Moderate for institutional participation; low-to-moderate for specific causal allocation
column7: Participation is well established; the scale and mechanism of his role in forced labor and famine harm require source-by-source inquiry. Do not infer that collaboration means sole responsibility or that it was merely tactical.
column8: Read Japanese occupation primary records, memoirs, local records, wartime labour/famine data and Sukarno's 1965 remarks.

column2: Indonesian independence was proclaimed by Sukarno and Hatta on 17 August 1945, two days after Japan's surrender; activist pressure and the debate over the proclamation's timing are part of the documented context.
column6: High for date and principal declarants; moderate for detailed sequence
column7: State Secretariat's page was not machine-readable in full; use contemporaneous text, BPUPKI/PPKI minutes and memoirs.
column8: Retrieve proclamation manuscript, radio/newspaper records and Rengasdengklok testimony.

column2: The United States did not control immediate Japanese surrender administration in most of Indonesia; British forces acting under Allied authority accepted surrender and handled the immediate return of Dutch forces.
column6: Moderate-high
column7: This is a U.S. retrospective account of its own role and British command arrangements; compare British and Dutch records.
column8: Review Allied command records and British/Indian troop records.

column2: U.S. policy toward Indonesian independence shifted over time: it moved from cautious/mediating positions to stronger pressure on the Netherlands by 1948–49, shaped partly by concern about communism and Western alliance politics.
column4: Official U.S. retrospective and primary policy documents
column6: High that U.S. policy documents state these motives; moderate as a complete account of actual policy
column7: FRUS is an official but selective U.S. publication; compare Dutch, Indonesian, British, Australian and UN archives.
column8: Map aid flows to Netherlands and leverage through ECA, UN, GOC/UNCI.

column2: After the December 1948 Dutch offensive, U.S. officials proposed Security Council action and possible ECA aid consequences to press release of prisoners and a transfer-of-sovereignty timetable.
column6: High for documented proposal
column7: A proposal and threat are not proof of the exact operational effect on Dutch decisions.
column8: Trace implementation, Dutch response and congressional/ECA records.

column2: The September 1948 Madiun events involved armed conflict, a takeover/change in regional administration, Sukarno's public broadcast against the movement, and a military-government campaign to restore central authority.
column4: Contemporary U.S. telegrams reproducing Indonesian government claims and reports
column6: Moderate-high for occurrence of conflict; lower for details in early diplomatic reporting
column7: Claims partly transmitted through government, press and intermediaries. Use neutral terminology until each local event is cross-checked.
column8: Compare Republic, PKI/FDR, military, Dutch intelligence, contemporary press and oral histories.

column2: Whether Madiun should be described primarily as a planned PKI coup, a response to army rationalization and factional conflict, or an escalating civil conflict remains contested in scholarship.
column6: High that interpretations are contested; no settled single causal explanation recorded
column7: Do not turn the Indonesian government's wartime label or an early U.S. telegram into a final factual verdict.
column8: Read full comparative studies and cited archives; distinguish chronology, agency, intention and retrospective memory.

column2: Madiun's suppression and the killing/capture of leading leftists became a precedent used by later anti-communist narratives; the event also materially affected U.S. views of Republican legitimacy.
column6: Moderate
column7: Specific death, capture and detention counts require primary evidence; later analogy does not prove continuity of command or policy.
column8: Build a name-level event ledger and map how army, party and school narratives changed over time.

column2: The 1955 DPR and Constituent Assembly were separate contests (29 September and 15 December). KPU's official historical table reports PKI 6,179,914 votes/16.36%/39 seats for DPR and 6,232,512/16.47%/80 seats for the Constituent Assembly. The four largest party lists' detailed totals are recorded separately in C078–C079.
column4: Official dynamic electoral portal and secondary index/search extracts
column6: High for the figures shown in KPU's published tables; original PPI tally records have not yet been inspected.
column7: KPU's directly opened official table separates both ballots; a 2018 regional-government history prints a 3,000 lower DPR PKI vote count, and ANRI archival-sourcebook tables are not yet readable from the retrieved PDF. Preserve the discrepancy.
column8: Inspect ANRI archival items and PPI final result tables; check the election commission's original official minutes and clarify BPS table metadata; C078–C079 preserve the complete KPU-published leading-party figures.

column2: U.S. records acknowledge approved covert political action and military aid for dissident regional movements in 1957–58, including air support and CAT pilots on combat missions.
column6: High for U.S. institutional admission; details of each sortie/chain still need triangulation
column7: The document records program-level authorization and activity but may omit implementation details; Pope's precise contractual relationship is not established here.
column8: Search CIA CREST/declassification files, NARA, Indonesian military/press, pilot records and regional command sources.

column2: U.S. and UK officials discussed covert-only action, recognition/secession options, and possible troops in April 1958; this document proves deliberation, not execution of those specific proposals.
column6: High
column7: Keep contemplated options distinct from actually supplied arms/air operations documented elsewhere.
column8: Trace minutes, approval records and any execution evidence.

column2: Presidential Decree No.150 of 5 July 1959 dissolved the Constituent Assembly and restored the 1945 Constitution, ending the 1950 provisional constitutional arrangement.
column6: High for decree text and institutional action
column7: Historical legality, political consent and downstream authoritarian effects are analytical questions.
column8: Compare court/assembly records, contemporaneous debate and constitutional scholarship.

column2: Indonesia enacted a sharecropping law (Law 2/1960), a national agrarian framework (Law 5/1960) and a landholding-limits instrument (Perpu 56/1960); their exact statutory provisions are now directly reviewed or checked against text reproductions, while local implementation remains open.
column6: High for enactment and stated law text; unresolved for local implementation
column7: UUPA and Perpu56 official BPK PDFs opened; Law2 text read in non-government transcription and cross-checked against official BPK metadata. Laws are not evidence of uniform enforcement or redistribution.
column8: Trace implementing regulations, district files, registration, compensation, beneficiaries and enforcement cases.

column2: A February 1965 U.S. 303 Committee paper records anti-PKI political-action work, liaison/support and propaganda mechanisms; some actions were ongoing while additional actions remained proposals, and the responsible agency name is partly redacted.
column6: High for contents as described in the released record
column7: Do not identify a redacted agency by guess; separate program approval, execution and effect.
column8: Seek unredacted copies, CIA/State files, budget records and evidence of Indonesian reception.

column2: On 20 July 1965 Rusk told the British Ambassador that the United States had decided to permit an approximately $3 million commercial sale of Army communications equipment after refusing an earlier $13 million request; the proposed fixed system was for Java sites. A 14 September NSC memorandum reported that the Army had rejected Philco's offer. Record this as a license decision followed by a reported rejection, not as delivered or installed equipment.
column4: Contemporaneous U.S. and UK records on commercial communications sales
column6: High for what the official records report; final licence, commercial contract, shipment and installation records have not been found.
column7: FRUS d127/d128; Hansard 29 July; FRUS d141. The U.S. and UK records describe different stages; d141 says the Army rejected the offer.
column8: Obtain the export-license file, Philco contract/cancellation and Indonesian Army communications records; establish formal license timing.

column2: A 6 October 1965 U.S. intelligence memorandum identified Untung, Suharto's role and an early leftist-coup hypothesis, but it is an initial intelligence assessment and does not prove PKI direction or Sukarno's responsibility.
column6: High for what the memo assessed; low as proof of its causal assertions
column7: Record the document's production date, information available and uncertainty, then compare later and non-U.S. records.
column8: Reconstruct event-hour chronology from Indonesian, U.S., British, Australian, Soviet and Chinese sources.

column2: A 22 October U.S. cable stated its role to date had been quiet assurance of non-interference; the same series records a 5 October plan for covert Army contact/anti-PKI messaging and a 14 October planned transfer of three radios, alongside February political action and November aid. Read the October statement as the Department's narrow outward posture, not a complete inventory of covert acts; the radio handover still lacks a separate receipt.
column4: Contemporary U.S. policy memo compared with adjacent records
column6: High for the memo's wording and series context
column7: FRUS d159 para 2 and Oct 5/14 records d147/d155; https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v26/d159
column8: Compare d147/d155 with d175/C193 and obtain October radio serials, transfer receipts and internal CIA/State operation files.

column2: November 1965 U.S. records document a proposed emergency communications program for selected anti-Communist Army leaders. FRUS d175 says the 19 November 303 Committee discussion favored assistance but sought more non-attributable surplus equipment before referral/approval; d211 later dates approval of the original proposal to 17 November, a discrepancy unresolved. The June 1966 follow-up says the original equipment was not provided as first proposed and records a separate February HF-link request, May equipment-availability notice, June technical briefings and June 24 approval of a further increment. The complete network is not shown as operational.
column4: Declassified U.S. records of proposal, committee discussion, later procurement and follow-up
column6: High for contents of official records; November approval date is inconsistent across d175/d211; actual receipt and full network operation remain unconfirmed.
column7: Keep the 17 Nov proposal, 19 Nov discussion, 17 Dec procurement, February request and June approval as distinct dated stages; equipment details remain redacted.
column8: Obtain 303 Committee minutes/action records for 17/19 Nov and 17 Dec, shipment records, recipient receipts, activation logs and Indonesian Army confirmations.

column2: U.S. records document transfer of lists of suspected PKI and related organization members to Indonesian authorities in late 1965; the list transfer is established, but its causal contribution to particular arrests or killings is not established by this evidence alone.
column4: Official FRUS editorial note based on released documents
column6: High for transfer; unresolved for direct effects
column7: Do not repeat claims about a 5,000-name list unless a source supporting that exact list is verified.
column8: Recover list copies, transmittal metadata, recipient accounts and named-person outcomes.

column2: A 26 October U.S. embassy analysis reportedly speculated about Chinese weapons or involvement in the September 30 Movement; this is an attributed U.S. assessment, not proof that China directed or armed it.
column6: Low for underlying allegation; high that an assessment existed
column7: Full passage not yet opened; keep this claim provisional and explicitly attributed.
column8: Open full document; seek Chinese, Indonesian, Soviet and third-country primary evidence.

column2: Scholarly literature commonly uses an approximate national death-toll range around several hundred thousand, often 400,000–500,000 or a broader range, but no precise national count is established; demographic methods cannot by themselves assign individual perpetrator responsibility.
column6: Moderate for broad scale; low for a precise number
column7: Abstract-only review so far; estimates and time/geographic boundaries differ by method.
column8: Read full methods, compare Indonesian demographic data, regional estimates and archival victim lists.

column2: Current scholarly work argues that military institutions encouraged, organized or facilitated violence, while patterns and civilian participation varied by region; the nationwide mechanism must be tested against local records.
column4: Peer-reviewed historical argument and regional study
column6: Moderate
column7: This is an analytical synthesis, not a single universally accepted formula; evidence currently reviewed is abstract-level.
column8: Build regional event datasets and compare orders, command structures, detention and local organizations.

column2: Soviet arms support during the 1962 West New Guinea crisis and Chinese-Indonesian political ties before 1965 are documented research subjects; neither fact alone establishes Soviet or Chinese direction of the September 30 Movement.
column6: High for need to separate earlier relations from 1965 causation
column7: Chinese working paper and Soviet-Indonesia study only partly reviewed.
column8: Trace contracts, delivery logs, leadership correspondence and 1965 diplomatic reporting.

column2: British information operations during Konfrontasi are a documented research subject, and Australian signals intelligence operated in the region; neither alone proves a domestic anti-PKI or killing operation in 1965.
column4: Peer-reviewed British study + official Australian history
column6: Moderate for existence of related regional activity; low for any direct link to domestic violence
column7: Linked declassified files and full articles have not yet been examined.
column8: Trace IRD/CAB/FCO/ASD records concerning Indonesia after 30 September and compare media output to operational orders.

column2: A World Bank/FRED annual CPI series reports extremely high Indonesian inflation in 1965 and a still higher figure in 1966, but the 1965 percentage cited by different publications varies with series and calculation.
column6: Moderate
column7: Do not quote a percentage without naming series, base, calculation and whether annual average or year-end rate.
column8: Compare BPS, Bank Indonesia and contemporary price series.

column2: ANRI has announced oral-history interviews with Sukarno's family and associates and has published archival finding aids; these are research gateways, not yet fully reviewed evidence.
column6: High for existence of program/catalogs; no substantive claims from unreviewed interviews
column7: Interview date, narrator, questioner, transcript and release restrictions must be recorded per item.
column8: Inventory every relevant transcript and archive file.

column6: Unresolved

column6: High for the existence and stated provisions of the law; unresolved for implementation
column7: The BPK official record and abstract were read and identify compensated nationalization and appeal provisions; the full promulgated legal text and enterprise-level application have not yet been verified.
column8: Retrieve the official gazette/full text, implementing lists, compensation cases and company-by-company control records.

column2: Sukarno and Inggit were married in 1923: ANRI's timeline says 24 April, while reporting from Inggit's heir on the family-held certificate says 24 March; Cambridge gives 1922. The year is better supported than the exact day/month.
column6: High for 1923; unresolved exact date
column7: ANRI describes marriage certificate No.1138 but does not expose a scan; family-reported certificate and ANRI timeline disagree by one month; Cambridge summary gives a different year.
column8: Inspect the certificate image/physical copy and underlying Bandung civil/administrative record; log provenance.

column6: High that ANRI reported these sources; contents not yet reviewed
column7: An archive-search report is not a substitute for the described records or interview transcript.
column8: Request item-level descriptions, reproduction permissions and transcript/audio metadata.

column2: ANRI's timeline places Sukarno in HBS in Surabaya from 1915 and living at Tjokroaminoto's home; it also records earlier schooling in Mojokerto and ELS.
column6: Moderate
column7: The chronology cites photographs/records in some entries; school registers have not yet been inspected directly.
column8: Compare ITB/HBS/ELS registers, family correspondence and Dutch education records.

column2: ANRI's timeline records a February 1929 letter in which Hatta urged Sukarno to limit political activity or leave temporarily and offered to prepare travel costs and accommodation in the Netherlands.
column6: Moderate
column7: Current evidence is the archive's curated chronology; the letter itself has not been opened.
column8: Locate and read the original letter, recipient copy, date, language, exact terms and subsequent response.

column2: The Indonesian Communist Party adopted the name PKI in May 1920; its organizational genealogy includes the earlier Indies Social Democratic Association founded in 1914, alongside Indonesian and transnational left networks.
column6: Moderate-high for institutional chronology
column7: Current evidence is scholarly catalogue/summary; inspect the relevant chapters and primary organizational records.
column8: Review ISDV/PKI constitutions, newspapers, colonial surveillance records and biographies of Semaoen, Tan Malaka, Darsono and Misbach.

column2: Dutch colonial land/labor regimes included the Java-centered Cultivation System from about 1830 and the 1870 Agrarian Law's state claim over uncultivated 'waste' land and long-term plantation concessions; effects varied by island, locality and labor regime.
column6: Moderate-high for broad legal/institutional summary
column7: The synthesis is secondary; Java, Sumatra and Outer Island histories differ. The exact statutory text and local implementation were not reviewed.
column8: Read original Dutch regulations, land concessions and regional labor/land histories.

column2: Pre-1965 Indonesian rural class structures should not be modeled as a homogeneous village: scholarship identifies landless laborers, share tenants, smallholders, petty landlords, village officials and region-specific plantation/work regimes.
column6: Moderate-high
column7: Current support is synthesis and selected regional article snippets; categories and balance vary in time and locality.
column8: Build locality-specific landholding, tenancy, wage, debt and state/estate data; compare contemporary survey records.

column2: A peer-reviewed study of Java's 1834–1879 Cultivation System estimates adverse mortality effects from forced labor using historical regional data; this is evidence about Java in the period studied, not a national or all-period mortality estimate.
column6: Moderate-high for study's reported result
column7: Causal estimates depend on data/model assumptions and apply to Java's Cultivation System; no direct inference to 1940s or 1960s.
column8: Read full methods, robustness checks, regional series and responses in the literature.

column2: A 2024 study attributes Java's 1944–45 food crisis to drought/delayed harvest interacting with Japanese rice quotas, below-market compensation under inflation and restrictions on inter-district food movement.
column4: Historical-economic synthesis supported by demographic study
column6: Moderate-high
column7: This establishes documented policy mechanisms as argued by the article; local enforcement, variation and actor-level responsibility need local records.
column8: Compare Japanese directives, residency reports, market prices, district harvest and mortality series.

column2: Van der Eng's 2024 published article estimates for Java a 3.3 million net population loss during 1942–45, including 1.8 million excess deaths and roughly 1.4 million missing births; the preceding working-paper abstract gives rounded 3.4 million and 1.9 million excess deaths. The earlier public 4 million figure includes speculative 1946 losses.
column6: Moderate for scale; not an exact death count
column7: Net population loss combines deaths and missing births; registration was incomplete, assumptions matter and geography is Java, not all Indonesia. Working paper and final article differ.
column8: Preserve versions, methods and geographic boundaries; compare census/vital records and earlier demographic studies.

column2: Published sources give different romusha denominators: one peer-reviewed article cites 2.6 million Java laborers and at least 200,000 deaths; a NIOD search result gives about 300,000 transported overseas and about 77,000 survivors. These likely refer to different populations and routes and must not be added or treated as a single census.
column6: Moderate for major forced mobilization; low-to-moderate for exact totals
column7: The peer-reviewed article cites earlier sources; NIOD's figures were visible in search snippet but not the page text. Japan's records were incomplete/destroyed.
column8: Trace underlying Huff/Sato/de Jong/Hovinga references, distinguish local vs overseas deployment, recruitment vs surviving returns.

column2: A recent historiographical article reports that in 1965 Sukarno accepted responsibility for romusha suffering but justified wartime cooperation as part of the route to independence.
column6: Moderate that the article reports it; exact wording/context unverified
column7: No speech transcript or recording has yet been read; translation and rhetorical context matter.
column8: Find the dated speech text/recording, original Indonesian wording, audience and contemporary reactions.

column2: A U.S. memorandum reports that Sukarno's 20 February 1959 speech announced a Cabinet decision to return to the 1945 Constitution and propose party-system simplification and parliamentary functional-group representation.
column6: High that the memorandum records this announcement; medium for the speech's full meaning absent transcript
column7: Secret contemporary U.S. memorandum quoting or summarizing local reporting; not an Indonesian Cabinet minute. The 5 July decree is separately registered at C018.
column8: Find the Indonesian speech, Cabinet minutes and Constituent Assembly debate; compare planned design with the decree actually issued.

column2: A September 1959 U.S. assessment says the first Guided Democracy Cabinet took office on 10 July, the Army was expanding its government role, Masyumi and PSI were excluded from the executive, and PKI participation remained limited; it interprets Sukarno as using the Army to counterbalance PKI power.
column4: Contemporary foreign diplomatic assessment and interpretation
column6: High for what the U.S. report stated; moderate for institutional facts; low-to-moderate for the U.S. interpretation of Sukarno's strategy
column7: Embassy/State Department analysis reflects U.S. access and strategic framing; verify cabinet lists, Indonesian minutes and Army appointments independently.
column8: Compare official cabinet rosters, military decrees, party press, Sukarno speeches and Indonesian participants' records.

column2: U.S. documents describe military aid as a multi-year program: the first $7m increment was essentially shipped by Dec 1958; a $15m second increment for Army shipments was expected to complete in Q1 FY1960; FY1960 had a presidential ceiling of $20m with $15m initially programmed, and a 1960 policy draft lists ceilings of $22m/$20m/$21m for FY1959/60/61.
column4: Foreign military-aid program: authorization, shipment status and ceilings distinguished
column6: High for U.S. records and program ceilings; moderate for reported shipment stage; causal effect not established
column7: A ceiling is not actual expenditure. Shipment status comes from U.S. internal reporting; no Indonesian receipt/inventory confirmation has yet been found.
column8: Reconcile grant/sale ledgers, program obligations, ship manifests, Indonesian Armed Forces inventories, units and training rosters.

column2: U.S. internal papers explicitly designed military assistance to improve internal security and counter Communist activity; the January 1959 recommendation called the Army the best prospect to stem Communist advances and said aid would strengthen Nasution and pro-West officers.
column6: High for stated U.S. intent; low for the program's independent causal contribution to Army behavior
column7: These papers directly establish how U.S. officials described objectives, not that their assumptions were correct or that aid caused later actions. FRUS d170 records a recommendation in January, before subsequent determinations.
column8: Compare U.S. policy with Indonesian command decisions, Army doctrine and other explanations for political/military alignments.

column2: On 5 December 1957 the Indonesian Cabinet decided to place Dutch enterprises already taken over by workers under government control and management boards; Foreign Ministry Secretary General Suwito told the U.S. ambassador this was temporary 'protective custody,' not confiscation or nationalization, and explained that workers and property protection were competing concerns.
column4: Contemporary report of Indonesian government explanation
column6: High that the telegram records Suwito's account; moderate for Cabinet decision; not an independent adjudication of motive or legal status
column7: The U.S. ambassador reports a conversation, not the Cabinet minutes. The quoted distinction was Suwito's explanation and should be compared with Indonesian orders and company records.
column8: Find the 5 December Cabinet resolution, military orders, union records and Dutch company/employee testimony.

column2: Indonesia's corporate-control sequence had distinct legal stages: PP 10/1958 created a central agency for Dutch industrial/mining companies and Indonesian managers; PP 23 and 24/1958 placed Dutch companies, including plantation/agricultural firms, under government control; Law 86/1958 later provided for nationalization of designated Dutch firms with compensation and Supreme Court appeal.
column6: High for legal instruments and dates recorded by official sources; moderate for practical control at individual firms
column7: The government's 1957–58 steps were not all legal nationalization. PP23/24 text extraction and firm-level operation remain incomplete; Law 86 delegates designation by later regulations.
column8: Build company-by-company timeline of worker action, Army takeover, management board, designation, compensation, ownership, labor outcomes and local receipts.

column2: The 1960 Basic Agrarian Law framed land as having a social function, prohibited ownership/control beyond limits, generally required active cultivation by the holder, and directed that surplus holdings be taken with compensation and distributed to people needing land; it also repealed named colonial agrarian provisions.
column6: High for statutory wording; not evidence that redistribution occurred
column7: Official legal text, PDF pages 0–5 and 23–24; legal reform was nationwide in form but land rights, customary status and implementation varied.
column8: Read drafting debates, implementing regulations, land-registration records and local outcomes by island/class.

column2: Law 2/1960 regulated food-crop sharecropping: it set an approximate 3-hectare maximum for sharecrop tenants absent special permission, required written agreements before the village head with two witnesses and camat approval, established minimum terms of three years for paddy and five for dry land, and left harvest shares to district-level determination under specified factors.
column4: Primary legal text / statutory regulation of labor and tenancy
column6: High for text reproduced and BPK metadata; practice unverified
column7: The full transcription was read on a non-government host; compare to the original State Gazette. Formal rules do not establish compliance or bargaining power.
column8: Compare district ratio decrees, village contracts, court cases, oral histories and local labor/tenancy records.

column2: Perpu 56/1960 set a general family ceiling of 20 hectares (with a limited exceptional increase), prohibited excessive holdings and directed the Government to work toward each farm family having at least two hectares; excess acquisition was tied to compensation and later distribution. It became effective 1 January 1961.
column6: High for statutory text; regional implementation and later sub-ceilings require further legal review
column7: The national instrument sets the general rule; later implementing rules specify regional criteria. Do not infer that every family received two hectares.
column8: Read PP 224/1961 and regional regulations, excess-land lists, compensation files and actual distribution records.

column2: The explanatory memorandum to Perpu 56/1960 states the government's estimate that about 60% of Indonesian farmers were landless and describes smallholders, sharecroppers, wage laborers, land held through mortgages/rents and large concentrations of control.
column4: Contemporary official socioeconomic estimate and rationale
column6: High that the official text states this figure and analysis; low-to-moderate as a population estimate until independently validated
column7: The figure is part of the regulation's policy explanation; it is not a modern audited census. The memorandum itself notes control through gadai and rent beyond registered ownership.
column8: Locate the original survey/statistical series behind the estimate; compare with BPS and contemporaneous agricultural/land surveys by region.

column2: A 1972 scholarly study reports that the land-reform apparatus created in 1961 ran from a presidentially headed Central Committee through provincial, regency, district and village committees; civil administrators and security officials held central positions, while peasant organizations had limited representation and local landholder interests could dominate.
column6: Moderate; author cites Presidential Decree 131/1961 and contemporary World Bank material
column7: Secondary reconstruction with dated statistics and selective locality coverage; does not establish uniform composition or capture in all districts.
column8: Obtain Presidential Decree 131/1961 and regional committee rosters/minutes; compare Central/East Java, Bali and Sumatra.

column2: Research on the PKI/BTI describes a strategic shift around 1953–54 from land nationalization and collective cultivation toward landlord-land redistribution to peasants as private owners; by 1961 the PKI peasant conference publicly pressed the government to implement the 1960 sharecropping, agrarian and land-ceiling laws.
column4: Party strategy and primary organizational demand
column6: Moderate-high for the publicly recorded party position; local practice and internal debates need original records
column7: The 1961 conference text is an online transcription without the original pamphlet; scholarly interpretation of the earlier shift cites party documents. Public platform is not proof of complete organizational consensus.
column8: Find original conference pamphlet, party congress records, local BTI minutes, land claims and opposing organizations' records.

column2: The 1962 Gerwani rural program, as quoted in a peer-reviewed agrarian-history article, included women's participation in village meetings and office, women's right to own land, higher agricultural wages and registration of moneylenders to address debt.
column4: Gendered rural political program, reported by scholarship
column6: Moderate; article cites Gerwani's 1962 conference publication, original pamphlet not yet opened
column7: Do not reduce Gerwani's rural platform to a PKI land program; its demands connect gender, work, local governance and credit.
column8: Locate the original 1962 Gerwani conference volume, regional women's-group records and village implementation evidence.

column2: A peer-reviewed synthesis argues that when implementation stalled, BTI undertook sporadic unilateral land occupations in 1963; Sukarno opposed those actions and prohibited them and related polemic in June 1964, then publicly welcomed BTI delegates and expressed support for peasants in September 1964.
column4: Later scholarly account of policy conflict and political alignment
column6: Moderate; article cites earlier scholarship and Sukarno's 1964 speech, but primary decrees/speech not yet inspected
column7: The article's characterization is not a complete locality-by-locality count. This sequence shows policy conflict but does not by itself establish Sukarno's motive or the consequences for 1965.
column8: Locate the June 1964 directive and original speech transcript; compare BTI records and local action/repression by district.

column2: Presidential Decrees 200 and 201 dated 17 August 1960 formally ordered dissolution of Masyumi and PSI respectively; BPK records the Masyumi decree, and an ANRI-attributed scan is available for the PSI decree.
column6: High for existence, title and date; detailed grounds and implementation need direct transcription
column7: BPK PDF viewer did not expose OCR; the ANRI SIKN origin page for the PSI scan was inaccessible, so the Commons image is an access copy with stated provenance. The decree grounds are not assessed here.
column8: Transcribe both originals; read the 1959 Party Regulation, correspondence with party leaders, Supreme Court/administrative records and branch-level implementation.

column2: ANRI's Presidentpedia biography and Cambridge's summary place Sukarno's birth on 6 June 1901 in Surabaya and name his parents as Raden Soekemi Sosrodihardjo and Ida Ayu Nyoman Rai.
column4: Biographical fact attributed to curated and scholarly biographies
column6: High for the reported birth date and parent names; archival record not yet inspected
column7: Two biographical sources agree on the broad facts. The ANRI page is a curated biography and the underlying civil/family records have not been retrieved.
column8: Locate civil, school, family and colonial records and compare spelling, dates and source provenance.

column2: ANRI reports that Sukarno attended school in Surabaya, lodged in H.O.S. Tjokroaminoto's household, then studied at HBS and THS in Bandung; this documents an important early personal and political network lead.
column6: Moderate-high that the sources report this sequence; exact dates and household arrangement need original records
column7: The relationship is described in retrospective biographies and the curated ANRI page; it does not by itself establish the extent of ideological influence, patronage or family intimacy.
column8: Inspect Surabaya and Bandung enrollment/grade records, household correspondence, Tjokroaminoto family papers and Dutch surveillance/court materials.

column2: A 1953 U.S. policy supplement states that Indonesia's 5 January 1952 MSA assurances were widely suspected of compromising independent foreign policy and contributed to the fall of the Sukiman Cabinet; it records a 12 January 1953 replacement agreement continuing economic grants while discontinuing grant military aid.
column4: U.S. government account of aid agreement and domestic political reaction
column6: High that the U.S. memorandum records this sequence; moderate for its causal account of the Cabinet's fall
column7: The evidence is a U.S. internal retrospective/progress report. It does not substitute for Indonesian Cabinet records, parliamentary debate or public opinion evidence.
column8: Compare Indonesian Foreign Ministry/Cabinet files, parliamentary proceedings, press and the original MSA notes.

column2: The U.S. NSC's November 1953 Indonesia policy directed officials to use personal influence (especially on Sukarno), economic and technical aid and rubber/tin markets, military training/equipment for internal security, information and person-exchange programs, and expanded intelligence collection.
column3: 1953 policy; implemented status varies by instrument
column6: High for the stated policy instruments; not evidence that each instruction was implemented or effective
column7: The directive is strong evidence of intent and authorized channels. Implementation, recipients, budgets, field activity and Indonesian response require separate records.
column8: Match each channel to agency budgets, Embassy and CIA files, aid/training/exchange rosters, recipients, press products and Indonesian records.

column2: A November 1957 U.S. memorandum reported 395 Indonesian officers trained at U.S. service schools since 1950 and 96 further slots for that year; it recommended responding to an Indonesian equipment request partly to strengthen pro-U.S. military elements and influence army orientation.
column6: High that the memorandum reports the figures and rationale; delivery and recipient-level effects remain unverified
column7: The source is an internal U.S. recommendation; the 395 count is an official claim, while the 96 were available slots. Recommendations for token shipments and equipment selection were not themselves deliveries.
column8: Find U.S. training rosters, Indonesian officer biographies, equipment contracts/shipments, academy curricula and Indonesian military inventories.

column2: An April 1961 White House briefing retrospectively stated that U.S. policy had supported anti-Communist opposition, backed the 1957–58 Outer Islands rebellion during a short period, and later extended military assistance to and encouraged political cooperation with Nasution's Army as a non-Communist force.
column4: U.S. internal policy retrospective; compare with U.S. operational records
column6: High that U.S. officials recorded this policy interpretation; high at program level when read with S020; exact operational chains and effects still require corroboration
column7: The briefing is a candid but interested U.S. account prepared for the Sukarno visit. It simplifies internal policy debates and does not describe all Indonesian/regional agency or variation.
column8: Compare CIA/NARA operational files, U.S. funding/delivery records, Taiwan/GRC records, Indonesian Army/rebel archives and regional testimony.

column2: In April 1961 U.S. briefing papers considered a trusteeship approach and stronger U.S. persuasion with the Dutch over West New Guinea; in the meeting record Sukarno pressed Kennedy to recognize Indonesia's claim and argued that U.S. post-1950 policy seemed less supportive of Indonesian national aspirations.
column4: Diplomatic proposal and recorded leader-to-leader exchange
column6: High that U.S. papers and meeting memorandum record these positions; the memorandum is not verbatim
column7: The U.S. file captures its own proposed language and record of Sukarno's statements. It does not independently adjudicate West New Guinea's legal status, local consent or the effects of the exchange.
column8: Compare Indonesian meeting notes, Sukarno/Subandrio speeches, Dutch and Australian records, UN debates and subsequent diplomacy.

column2: A 2018 Yogyakarta-government election history reports PKI's 1955 DPR vote total as 6,176,914, while KPU's official historical table reports 6,179,914 (a 3,000-vote difference); the regional book cites Feith (1957), so this is an unresolved transmission/edition discrepancy pending the PPI tally.
column6: High that the two publications differ; high that KPU's own table prints 6,179,914; underlying official PPI tally still open
column7: The difference is visible in directly opened table passages. Do not silently average, normalize or attribute the discrepancy to fraud; a transcription error is plausible but not yet established.
column8: Inspect ANRI/Kempen and Cabinet Presidential archive items, PPI final tables and original result announcement records; compare Feith's printed table.

column2: A 20 October 1952 U.S. embassy cable reports that, after a Jakarta demonstration, senior Army officers led by Nasution presented Sukarno, Hatta and Prime Minister Wilopo with a written petition to dissolve Parliament and transfer governing authority to the President; the ambassador says much of his 'inside story' came from President's Secretary/Chef de Cabinet Pringgo Digdo under a protection request.
column4: Contemporaneous diplomatic report with identified insider source chain
column6: High that the U.S. cable records the described sequence; moderate for exact reconstruction pending Indonesian and army-side originals
column7: The telegram is top secret, restricts distribution to protect its named informant, combines Pringgo's account with other embassy reporting, and notes that the written petition itself was not printed. It is not a verbatim transcript or a court finding.
column8: Find the petition, Indonesian Cabinet/Parliament minutes, police/army logs, Sukarno's and Nasution's accounts, Jakarta newspapers and independent studies.

column2: In an October 1952 meeting report, Sukarno attributed the palace crowd to young Army officers/civilians linked to or influenced by PSI, Murba members and pro-dictatorship figures; he said the Irian issue helped disperse it and expressed respect and affection for Sultan Hamengkubuwono IX while rejecting press claims of a personal dispute with the Sultan.
column4: Reported private leader-to-ambassador conversation and personal/political relationship
column6: High that the ambassador's memorandum attributes these remarks to Sukarno; moderate-to-low as a complete account of the crowd or the Sultan's own views
column7: This is Cochran's paraphrase, not a stenographic record. It preserves Sukarno's presentation and concern about foreign press reports; it does not independently verify the crowd's composition or prove no disagreement existed.
column8: Compare Sultan's own papers, Indonesian press and government statements, Sukarno's speeches, palace/Army reports and Dutch/UK records.

column2: A State Department intelligence estimate dated 2 March 1954 describes the October 17 affair as a military challenge to Parliament and identifies an intra-Army conflict between advocates of a small modern professional army and those favoring retention of a larger force containing revolutionary guerrilla/irregular elements.
column6: High that OIR stated this assessment; moderate as an explanation of Indonesian Army factions
column7: The report was an OIR contribution to NIE-65-54 and explicitly states that it is intelligence, not departmental policy. It is a U.S. assessment with limited access and Cold War assumptions, not neutral proof of all officers' motives.
column8: Compare Indonesian Army rosters, Nasution and Simatupang texts, parliamentary debates, Indonesian newspapers and scholarship using local records.

column2: Hatta's 20–21 July 1956 resignation letters, as quoted in later institutional and university publications, tied his departure to the elected DPR and Constituent Assembly beginning work and argued that a vice-presidency was unnecessary under a parliamentary cabinet system; later institutional synthesis separately notes differences with Sukarno. Keppres No. 13 was issued 5 February 1957 but made effective from 1 December 1956.
column4: Reported primary correspondence plus official legal chronology and later interpretation
column6: High for Keppres's effective date and the published letter wording; moderate for how formal constitutional reasoning and political disagreement combined
column7: The original letters and Cabinet/DPR minutes have not yet been directly inspected. The Constitutional Court compilation cites Mavis Rose for Sukarno-Hatta differences; do not reduce the departure to a personal feud or a single cause.
column8: Retrieve original Hatta letters of 20–21 July, DPR and Cabinet minutes, 1956 correspondence, Hatta memoir and Mavis Rose's referenced pages.

column2: A 26 December 1956 U.S. embassy telegram reports Hatta as saying he was concerned about his wife's illness and wanted a quieter life, while still consulting Simatupang and leaders of multiple parties; Hatta reportedly favored a presidential cabinet formed by Sukarno during the Sumatra crisis.
column4: Contemporaneous report of private political conversation and network contacts
column6: High that the cable records these statements and contacts; moderate for the paraphrased content; no independent measure of private motives
column7: The cable is the ambassador's paraphrase. It records Hatta's reported interaction with political and military actors, but not a verbatim interview and not a complete explanation for his resignation.
column8: Seek Hatta's private letters, diaries/memoirs, Simatupang and party-leader papers, Indonesian press and Cabinet records.

column2: The 1957 emergency-law record distinguishes at least three legal steps: Keppres 40 declared the whole territory including territorial waters in a state of emergency/war on 14 March; the December 1957 Keppres 225 declaration was ratified by Law 79; Law 74/1957 supplied a statutory state-of-danger framework; Perpu 23/1959 repealed Law 74 and defined civil-emergency, military-emergency and war levels with broad powers over meetings, publications, movement, property and detention.
column4: Primary legal acts and statutory framework
column6: High for the texts and official metadata; no inference about the extent or legality of actual implementation
column7: The March and December 1957 declarations are separate instruments. Statutory powers show formal authority only; actual orders, orders of battle, arrests, censorship and local practice require separate evidence.
column8: Inspect the full Keppres 40 and 225 scans, state-of-war orders, regional commander orders, implementing regulations, court files and local press/arrest records.

column2: A secret U.S. State Department profile says U.S. military observers had been on close friendly terms with Nasution during his first Army Chief of Staff tenure and says Army officer training in U.S. service schools began under Nasution; this records an American relationship and claimed institutional channel, not proof of policy obedience or U.S. control.
column4: Contemporary foreign diplomatic assessment of military and personal networks
column6: High that the U.S. memorandum records the relationship and its own program history; moderate pending Indonesian-side roster/correspondence verification
column7: The profile is interested U.S. reporting and uses its own pro-West/anti-Communist classifications. The 1957 assistance memo (S096) separately gives a count of officers trained; neither source proves resulting political control.
column8: Compare U.S. and Indonesian officer rosters, training files, letters, Nasution's memoirs, course records and evidence of officers trained by other states.

column2: The same 1958 U.S. profile identifies Nasution and Zulkifli Lubis as first cousins and attributes part of their hostility and later military conflict to a rivalry it says dated at least to the October 17 affair; the relationship is a verifiable family-history lead, while the motive claim remains uncorroborated U.S. analysis.
column4: Reported kinship and attributed personal motive
column6: Moderate that the report identifies them as first cousins; low for the claimed causal role of personal hostility
column7: The memorandum names no informant for the family relationship or motive in the published text. Its psychological and causal language is strongly evaluative.
column8: Verify kinship through family records, Indonesian/Batak biographies, Nasution and Lubis correspondence, Army appointment/purge records and independent scholarship.

column8: Obtain Critchley's reply, Malaysian cabinet/defense orders, British operational logs and Indonesian redeployments.
