column2: The 1 July 1965 interagency NIE assessed that the PKI’s role in the Indonesian government had accelerated over the previous year and was likely to continue while Sukarno remained in control; this was a forecast, not retrospective evidence of October’s later course.
column6: High for the estimate’s text; the underlying characterization and forecast accuracy are unverified.
column7: FRUS d126, published conclusions; the discussion section was omitted. The estimate predates the September 30 Movement and does not establish what happened later.
column8: Obtain the full NIE discussion and compare with Indonesian party/government records and non-U.S. diplomatic reporting.

column2: Rusk told British Ambassador Dean the U.S. had decided to permit about $3m in commercial communications equipment for the Indonesian Army after rejecting a $13m request.
column6: High for meeting statement
column7: Not evidence of shipment or Indonesian receipt.
column8: Locate export license Philco contract and shipping/receipt records.

column2: A July 20 instruction described fixed troposcatter systems for Jakarta Bandung and Palembang; U.S. asserted these would not support confrontation against Malaysia.
column6: Moderate-high for cited instruction
column7: Original telegram 46 not opened; geography contradicts loose claim of Java-only equipment.
column8: Obtain telegram 46 and installation plans.

column2: Dean protested July 28 that the U.S. license undermined British efforts to restrict military sales to Indonesia; Rusk defended internal Army communications.
column6: High for meeting statements
column7: No evidence of actual sale or downstream effects.
column8: Check British Foreign Office record and Indonesian procurement.

column2: August 2 editorial note reports Rusk doubted Indonesia would complete the communications purchase.
column6: Moderate; cited meeting not opened
column7: August 2 memorandum absent.
column8: Obtain August 2 conversation and purchase records.

column2: On August 3 Blouin proposed reconsidering the Philco licence, unannounced U.S. naval passage through Indonesian straits, continued Atlantis II survey work outside claimed territorial waters, and preparation for the political effects of a possible Indonesian nuclear test. These were proposals, not orders.
column6: High for the recommendations in the memorandum; no approval or execution is established.
column7: FRUS d129, text and notes. Blouin’s judgments about Indonesian motives and possible nuclear activity remain attributed assessments.
column8: Find follow-up authorization, ship and survey logs, Philco licence records, and nuclear monitoring tasking.

column2: On August 3 Cooper and Thomson advised against panic-driven evacuation or mission reductions before August 17 and said Ambassador Green should guide the dependents’ evacuation decision; the FRUS note reports that Green opposed closing the Medan and Surabaya posts.
column4: NSC policy advice with an editorially reported Embassy position
column6: High for Cooper and Thomson’s advice; the account of Green’s position is secondary through the FRUS editorial note.
column7: FRUS d130 and its editorial note; underlying July 30/August 7 consular cables and August 9 memorandum were not directly read.
column8: Obtain the cited consular cables and August 9 memorandum; compare with the Embassy’s evacuation, staffing and closure decisions.

column2: The July estimate forecast continuing hostility toward the United States while judging a diplomatic break to be less than even likely.
column6: High for the forecast as printed; not a measure of Indonesian public opinion.
column7: U.S. intelligence forecast based on omitted discussion; do not treat likelihood as an observed fact.
column8: Compare Indonesian Foreign Ministry records and later diplomatic actions.

column2: The same estimate expected closer Indonesia–China ties and relatively friendly ties with the USSR, partly because Indonesian military leaders wanted Soviet arms assistance.
column6: High that the estimate made this forecast; actual intent and arms flows need separate verification.
column7: Does not establish Chinese/Soviet decisions, quantities, delivery or Indonesian receipt.
column8: Compare Indonesian, Chinese and Soviet diplomatic and arms records.

column2: CINCPAC’s 1965 command history says deterioration in U.S.–Indonesia relations led to deletion of FY1965 MAP funds for the fixed communications project and suspension of further electronic-equipment deliveries in March.
column6: High that the command history records these decisions; underlying cables and accounting entries remain to check.
column7: The history cites contemporaneous Defense and State messages not opened here.
column8: Obtain cited CINCPAC/OSD/State cables and FY1965 MAP budget and storage records.

column2: CINCPAC says agencies debated cancellation versus continuing to delay delivery and describes a general tactic of delay and non-delivery while State judged the political climate unsuitable.
column6: High that the history describes the debate; moderate that it captures all institutional views.
column7: Defense institutional summary based on cited records not opened.
column8: Inspect cited State, OSD, CINCPAC and Embassy messages and minutes.

column2: CINCPAC records MILTAG was replaced by a seven-person Defense Liaison Group effective Sept. 1, 1965, to retain personal contact with the armed forces, MAP files and limited rapid-start capacity.
column4: Retrospective military command history of liaison reorganization
column6: High for the U.S. organizational decision as recorded; Indonesian access and contact frequency remain unverified.
column7: Command History p.174; Joint Chiefs notification not opened.
column8: Find the order, Embassy roster, DLG reports and Indonesian liaison records.

column2: CINCPAC reported roughly $66 million in MAP items, including small arms, vehicles and radios, had been delivered since 1960, while DLG lacked capacity to inventory the Army’s in-country equipment.
column4: U.S. military assistance summary and inventory limitation
column6: High that CINCPAC reported this rounded figure; aggregate and delivery status require item-level validation.
column7: Command History pp.178–179 provides no serial-level list or Indonesian receipt records.
column8: Reconcile MAP contracts and shipment/end-use records with Indonesian Army inventories.

column2: The communications project originally envisaged twelve sites; by 1965 the reduced commercial completion focused on Jakarta, Bandung and Palembang.
column6: High for U.S./UK records’ project descriptions; construction and operating status at each site need checking.
column7: Sources describe different stages; no evidence here confirms three functioning stations.
column8: Inspect engineering reports, Philco schedules and Indonesian communications records.

column2: CINCPAC says Yani tentatively chose direct commercial arrangements with Philco, which Washington accepted as the only available option; State authorized negotiations for three sites and refused twelve because of Konfrontasi.
column4: Retrospective account of U.S. approval conditions and Army preference
column6: High that the command history records the choices and conditions; contract execution is not established.
column7: Underlying Yani and Philco correspondence remains unread.
column8: Obtain the export file, Yani message, Philco offer and Army procurement minutes.

column2: CINCPAC reports Philco declined to contract for any sites or operate the temporary link commercially, while the Indonesian Army did not want only three sites.
column4: Retrospective report of failed commercial negotiations
column6: High that the history records the breakdown; underlying letters remain missing.
column7: FRUS d141 separately reports the Army rejection but provides no letter.
column8: Find Philco correspondence, the Army response and temporary-link logs.

column2: CINCPAC says the Philco contract was terminated in September, MAP-purchased equipment in California was reassigned to Thailand, and the temporary Jakarta–Bandung link was left for Indonesian use.
column4: Retrospective command history of cancellation and equipment disposition
column6: High that U.S. command history reports these actions; link operation and Indonesian receipt need verification.
column7: Underlying Army, OSD, CINCPAC and Embassy messages were not opened.
column8: Obtain termination and transfer orders, warehouse manifests, maintenance logs and Indonesian receipts.

column2: On Aug. 2, 1965 the UK Foreign Secretary told the Commons that the U.S. export licence remained under consideration and Britain opposed improving Indonesian Army capability while Konfrontasi continued.
column6: High for the UK public statement; not the final U.S. licence decision.
column7: Distinct from Rusk’s July 20 internal description of a decision to permit sale.
column8: Locate U.S. Commerce licence file, UK diplomatic representations and Philco correspondence.

column2: A July 21 State INR memorandum said Pakistan had reportedly supplied the Indonesian Air Force C-130 replacement parts in late June from U.S.-supplied stocks; Rusk repeated the allegation to Britain on July 28.
column4: Contemporaneous report of alleged third-country retransfer
column6: High that U.S. officials recorded the allegation; low-to-moderate that transfer occurred without recipient/shipment evidence.
column7: Hughes labels the memo informal and based on sensitive sources; the reports may share a channel and are not independent confirmation.
column8: Find Pakistani export/end-use files, part serials and Indonesian Air Force maintenance and receipt books.

column2: U.S. records reported that the Medan consulate was stoned on July 30, 1965.
column4: Contemporaneous U.S. diplomatic report of an attack
column6: High that U.S. officials reported the incident; organizers and police response need Indonesian corroboration.
column7: The telegram itself was not opened; do not treat “Communist-led” as verified attribution.
column8: Obtain Medan telegram 3, Indonesian press/police records and eyewitness accounts.

column2: An FRUS editorial note says Surabaya Consulate was attacked Aug. 7 and quotes an Aug. 9 memo that Indonesian security forces did their best to restrain the crowd.
column4: Incident relayed through documentary editorial note
column6: Moderate-high for attack as reported; moderate for security-force characterization pending the memo.
column7: Cited Aug. 9 memo was not opened; no local police record yet.
column8: Obtain Aug. 9 NSC memo, consular cables, police and press records.

column2: On Aug. 8 the State Department froze movement of U.S. Government personnel to Indonesia, ordered a plan to reduce the Embassy to essential staff, and asked Medan and Surabaya to assess danger against consular utility.
column6: High for the decision and instruction; implementation levels and timing require rosters.
column7: The memo gives no final staffing numbers.
column8: Inspect Embassy and consular rosters and later travel orders.

column2: Sukarno stated on July 24, 1965 that Indonesia would build its own atomic bomb in the near future, according to a U.S. Defense memorandum.
column4: Report of a public political statement
column6: High that the memorandum attributes this statement to Sukarno; underlying speech/report should be located.
column7: Not evidence of a technical program or successful bomb development.
column8: Find speech transcript, Antara coverage and Indonesian defense/scientific files.

column2: Defense officials reported Hartono had said 200 scientists were working on a bomb and forecast an October “surprise,” then described a possible test after the Algiers conference.
column4: Report of military official’s nuclear statements
column6: High that the U.S. memo reports these statements; low for the underlying technical program.
column7: Reported remarks are not technical indicators; original speeches and source records were not opened.
column8: Retrieve Hartono speeches, Army Arsenal records, staffing and equipment files.

column2: The Defense memo judged Indonesia could not produce a bomb without outside assistance, considered propaganda and Chinese-cooperation scenarios, and asked DIA to monitor indicators and coordinate with Britain.
column4: U.S. capability assessment and monitoring plan
column6: High for U.S. assessment and plan; low for actual Indonesian capability or Chinese involvement.
column7: U.S. contingency planning is not proof of test preparation.
column8: Seek DIA/British monitoring, Indonesian technical files and independent test-site evidence.

column2: At an Aug. 18 meeting George Ball said Sukarno’s Aug. 17 speech aligned Indonesia with Communist-world objectives and said Sukarno had aided PKI penetration of government.
column6: High that Ball expressed this view; low as a measure of Indonesian alignment or PKI penetration.
column7: A single official’s interpretation; the speech and Indonesian response require direct reading.
column8: Compare Indonesian speech, cabinet, party, press and other diplomatic records.

column2: Green reported different readings of Sukarno’s Aug. 17 speech, attributing a mild interpretation to Australians, Britons and Indians and saying some Indonesian Army officers and businesspeople downplayed it.
column6: High that Green recorded these attributions; moderate-to-low for representativeness.
column7: Green identifies few sources and provides no survey.
column8: Read the Australian report and British, Indian, Indonesian Army, business and press responses.

column2: Green recommended maintaining contact with Indonesian military and other power groups, diplomatic and consular presence, and political, economic and intelligence reporting for a post-Sukarno period.
column6: High for recommendation; no inference about completion or later influence.
column7: Policy advice is not proof of implementation or effect.
column8: Check staffing orders, DLG reports and subsequent U.S. decision memoranda.

column2: Green recommended publicity through third countries, VOA and Embassy bulletins, while expecting limited effect.
column6: High for proposal and stated expectation; implementation and reception unverified.
column7: Not a broadcast log, script, partner action or audience study.
column8: Find VOA/USIA schedules, scripts, partner records and reception evidence.

column2: The FRUS editor’s note recounts William Bundy’s later account that Ball asked whether CIA assets could reverse Indonesia’s political direction and a CIA representative replied assets were weak and unlikely to have much impact.
column4: Retrospective recollection in an official documentary edition
column6: Moderate that Bundy later recounted this; low-to-moderate for exact wording and CIA capability.
column7: The specific exchange comes through a later foreword and 1995 recollection, not a contemporary CIA record; it does not cover all operations.
column8: Read Bundy’s full foreword and 1995 transcript; seek contemporary and CIA records.

column2: The Sept. 1 SNIE said the PKI claimed three million members and characterized it as Indonesia’s best-organized and most dynamic political entity.
column4: Intelligence assessment citing party membership claim
column6: High that the estimate says this; membership and comparative judgment are not independently verified.
column7: It labels the total as a PKI claim and the ranking as U.S. analysis.
column8: Find PKI membership and dues registers and provincial counts.

column2: The Sept. 1 SNIE forecast that if Sukarno remained in power the PKI might gain enough state influence in two or three years for Indonesia to be termed a Communist state.
column6: High for the forecast; not evidence it came true.
column7: The source note says approved Sept. 10; forecast rests on U.S. assumptions and omitted discussion.
column8: Compare with Indonesian institutional records and underlying estimate.

column2: The SNIE forecast an initial non-Communist coalition after Sukarno’s early death or incapacity, with the PKI retaining an important share and the military unlikely to risk civil war for immediate rollback.
column6: High for the forecast; not a confirmed Army decision or actual outcome.
column7: Scenario estimate, not an observed succession plan.
column8: Compare underlying estimate with Indonesian succession plans and military records.

column2: Green reported that Sukarno criticized U.S. media, named Time, Life and Newsweek, and said anti-U.S. feeling and demonstrations would continue while U.S. publications defamed Indonesia and its leaders.
column6: High that Green recorded this; exact wording moderate because no transcript exists.
column7: The report is not a verbatim record and does not establish public opinion or media effects.
column8: Find Indonesian/U.S. meeting notes, Sukarno’s records and the cited media coverage.

column2: Green assessed that the Aug. 31 meeting with Sukarno achieved little beyond establishing rapport.
column6: High that Green made this assessment; not a measure of Sukarno’s private response.
column7: The judgment is one participant’s view.
column8: Compare later meeting reports and Indonesian accounts.

column2: On Sept. 10 State suspected a PKI-led campaign and possible central-government collusion or tacit approval behind pressure on U.S. consulates, while acknowledging other motives and possible provincial inability to control extremists.
column4: U.S. policy assessment with stated alternatives
column6: High for U.S. suspicion and caveats; low for coordination absent Indonesian command evidence.
column7: The telegram explicitly says “suspect” and recognizes alternative explanations.
column8: Open cited telegrams 598/609 and seek local organizers, police orders and government correspondence.

column2: Rusk instructed the Embassy to demand a security guarantee and said the United States intended to close Surabaya Consulate without one; he ordered contingency planning to move staff and destroy classified material.
column6: High for instruction; does not establish closure or destruction occurred.
column7: Distinguish conditional threat and preparation from implementation.
column8: Find Embassy response, later orders, property logs and evacuation records.

column2: In the Sept. 10 meeting record Palar regretted attacks and said Sukarno allowed demonstrations to answer public sentiment but they sometimes got out of hand outside Jakarta.
column4: Attributed statement in diplomatic meeting record
column6: High that the U.S. memo records Palar saying this; explanation itself unverified.
column7: Palar’s account is not direct evidence of Sukarno’s orders or provincial police action.
column8: Open the Sept. 17 follow-up and compare Indonesian police/governor records.

column2: Rusk told Palar that U.S. relations required protection of American personnel and installations and warned Washington would examine Indonesian installations in the United States if U.S. operations became untenable.
column6: High for warning as recorded; no evidence reciprocal restrictions were applied.
column7: Conditional warning, not implemented closure or retaliatory action.
column8: Check subsequent U.S. decisions and Indonesian diplomatic correspondence.

column2: On Sept. 14 an NSC staff report said Subandrio had assured Green of U.S. personnel and property safety, while Washington remained skeptical.
column6: High that Thomson records Green’s report; independent Indonesian confirmation absent.
column7: Not Subandrio’s original written assurance.
column8: Obtain Green’s cable, Subandrio record and security measures.

column2: On 1 October, Ball asked McNamara to examine evacuation options for U.S. citizens, including ships already in the region and possible British or Australian aircraft at Singapore; McNamara understood the request to concern evacuation while the situation remained unclear.
column6: High that the officials discussed this contingency; not evidence ships or aircraft were moved or other action undertaken.
column7: FRUS d143, paragraphs 1–3. Ball said there were a couple thousand Americans across the islands and did not know whether any further action might follow once events clarified.
column8: Read the Oct. 1–4 Ball/Defense contingency calls and compare with CINCPAC movement logs, embassy evacuation orders and allied aircraft records.

column2: A later 1 October call recorded Ball asking CIA Director Helms whether the United States could categorically deny CIA operations involvement; Helms said Raborn had authorized a denial and that CIA had nothing to do with events.
column6: High that the edited FRUS note records Helms’s denial; this is not independent proof of the full scope of CIA activity.
column7: FRUS d143 editorial note 2 quotes Ball’s calls with Helms and says one line is not declassified. It records a statement about CIA operations in the Indonesia situation, not a full review of all U.S. contacts or prior policy programs.
column8: Seek the original Ball–Helms call memorandum, associated CIA/Director’s files and any separately authorized political-action records; preserve the withheld line as an unresolved gap.

column2: On the afternoon of 1 October, Ball told Fulbright that the apparent coup seemed leftist but that the extent of PKI involvement or foreknowledge remained uncertain; he also described incomplete reports of a counter-move and a possible Army return to the radio station.
column4: Contemporary U.S. official’s attributed report and assessment
column6: High for Ball’s recorded assessment; the underlying Indonesian reports and control of units are not independently established by this call.
column7: FRUS d144, paragraphs 1–4; the conversation is explicitly marked tentative and says the situation was difficult to know.
column8: Compare timestamped RRI transmissions, Indonesian Army and presidential orders, independent press, and other embassies’ same-day cables.

column2: On 2 October Ball told Rusk that reports pointed to Suharto’s forces gaining the upper hand and the PKI aligning with the losing side, while Sukarno’s status was still unknown; Rusk speculated that Sukarno might be dead or seriously ill.
column6: High that the officials exchanged these reports and guesses; not proof of the underlying military alignment or Sukarno’s actual status.
column7: FRUS d145, main text and editorial footnote 2. Green’s reported embassy assessment in the footnote also lists several competing explanations for Sukarno’s absence.
column8: Compare Sukarno’s diary and radio orders, presidential staff records, army command logs, and Indonesian press for the exact sequence.

column2: A 4 October Defense Department memorandum reported discovery of the senior officers’ bodies and recorded two incompatible U.S. hypotheses about whether Sukarno had prior knowledge or had been misled; Blouin leaned toward partial foreknowledge but presented this as his assessment.
column6: High for the memorandum’s competing theories and Blouin’s stated inclination; low for resolving Sukarno’s actual knowledge from this source alone.
column7: FRUS d146, paragraphs 1–2 and 4–8. It says some information was conflicting; reports of body condition and the Army’s use of the deaths are mediated through the memo.
column8: Compare independent autopsy records, contemporaneous RRI/press, Sukarno’s 1–4 October diary/letters, Air Force and presidential-guard records, and named participants’ testimony.

column2: The same 4 October memorandum placed U.S. naval task forces in positions described as possible emergency-evacuation cover and reported TF-76 moving north toward TF-77; it does not describe a combat mission in Indonesia.
column4: Contemporary U.S. military posture for civilian evacuation contingency
column6: High that the memorandum reports the positioning and stated contingency; exact track and purpose require operational logs.
column7: FRUS d146, evacuation section and editorial note 2, which says Ball, McNamara, McGeorge Bundy, William Bundy and Rusk discussed these forces on Oct. 3–4 for possible emergency evacuation.
column8: Obtain CINCPAC/Task Force 76 and 77 deck logs, tasking messages, and the Oct. 3–4 Ball papers; check distance from Indonesian waters.

column2: On 6 October State approved the broad guidelines in Green’s 5 October telegram but cautioned against public evidence that the U.S. supported the Army and advised against direct contact with Nasution unless he initiated it, favoring indirect access through senior officers already in contact with the Mission.
column4: U.S. diplomatic policy instruction and military liaison channel
column6: High for the written policy instruction; its receipt and execution in Jakarta need separate records.
column7: FRUS d148 paragraphs 1, 4–6, read with d147. d148 approves the main lines subject to emphasis and discretion, not every Green proposal as an executed action.
column8: Read the full Green telegram, Jakarta follow-up cables, ambassador contact logs and named senior-officer records.

column2: State said that the Army did not need U.S. material aid at that point and argued that years of training, civic-action work, MILTAG and repeated assurances to Nasution should already have established that the United States would support Army leaders if they needed help.
column4: U.S. official interpretation of prior military ties and reassurance
column6: High for State’s characterization of its own programs and intended signal; the Army’s independent understanding is not directly documented here.
column7: FRUS d148 paragraph 5. This statement concerns the immediate moment and does not establish that material support was never later provided.
column8: Compare MAP delivery and training records, MILTAG and DLG communications, Nasution’s papers, Army liaison logs and later aid requests/receipts.

column2: On 6 October State reported that a VOA and related information program was already being carried out by citing Indonesian sources and official statements without U.S. editorializing, with similar Indonesia coverage in selected broadcasts outside Indonesia; it planned to reconsider if those source materials dried up.
column4: U.S. information-program execution as reported by State
column6: High that State reported ongoing broadcast activity and its method; actual scripts, transmission reach, audience response and effects are unverified.
column7: FRUS d148 paragraph 6. The memo does not include VOA transmission logs or third-country station records. Distinguish this reported activity from Green’s covert Army-contact proposal in d147.
column8: Obtain VOA/Federal Broadcast Information Service logs, scripts, distribution schedules, USIA files and partner-station records; compare the cited Indonesian source statements.

column2: On 6 October the Department instructed the Embassy to begin moving U.S. families out of Indonesia on international commercial carriers and allowed routine home-leave or medical explanations at the outset to keep the operation unobtrusive.
column4: Contemporary evacuation instruction as cited in an official editorial note
column6: High that FRUS d150 footnote 2 reproduces the instruction’s gist; actual departures and the Embassy’s implementation roster are not shown.
column7: FRUS d150 footnote 2 cites Department telegram 401 to Djakarta, October 6, RG 59 POL 23–INDON; original cable not opened independently.
column8: Obtain telegram 401 and Embassy departure records, passenger manifests and family notifications.

column2: On 7 October Ball told Helms that Green had requested evacuation, commercial carriers were being used as unobtrusively as possible, and the target was for all dependents to depart within three weeks.
column6: High for Ball’s statement and the intended timeline; it does not establish that all dependents departed or where they went.
column7: FRUS d150, 12:05 p.m. telephone memorandum.
column8: Check Embassy travel rosters, airline manifests and later completion reports.

column2: In a 5:30 p.m. call on 7 October Ball and McNamara agreed that the evacuation task force could return slowly to home ports as the situation allowed; the note reports Ball feared civil war within two or three days.
column4: Contemporary contingency discussion, reported in an editorial footnote
column6: High for the call as summarized by FRUS; no ship movement, return route or final order is proved.
column7: FRUS d150 footnote 3 cites Johnson Library Ball Papers, telephone conversations on Indonesia.
column8: Obtain the original call memorandum, Defense movement orders and CINCPAC/TF76/TF77 logs.

column2: On 14 October Colonel Ethel delivered a U.S. oral message about Confrontation to a Nasution aide, who wrote it down and said he would pass it to Nasution; the aide said the reassurance would help the Army feel it was not being pressured from every side. An FRUS footnote cites an October 15 cable reporting that Nasution received the message and was very satisfied, hoping Britain would “lay off.”
column4: Reported diplomatic message transmission and recipient reaction
column6: High that the U.S. record reports message delivery and Nasution’s reported reaction; no Indonesian recipient minute, British response or policy effect is independently checked.
column7: FRUS d154 paragraph 1 and footnote 3, which cites Department telegram 2005 to London, October 15; d151/C750 supplies context for the original reassurance.
column8: Retrieve telegram 2005, Jakarta 1006, British FO response and any Nasution or Indonesian command record.

column2: An unnamed Nasution aide told Green that the Army was rounding up Chinese businessmen suspected of involvement and trying to determine the Chinese Embassy’s role in the September 30 events; this is a second-hand U.S. report, not proof of the suspects’ conduct or Beijing’s role.
column4: Attributed Army contact report concerning Chinese Indonesians and China
column6: High for what the U.S. cable records; low for the underlying allegation, legal basis, scale or result.
column7: FRUS d154 paragraph 2; unnamed aide relayed the statements through Ethel.
column8: Check Indonesian arrest and court files, Chinese Embassy records, local Chinese-community testimony and reports from other embassies.

column2: The same aide reported that Army units were rounding up Communist cadres but having difficulty locating weapons said to have been distributed; no quantity, recipient list or seizure inventory is provided.
column4: Attributed Army liaison report of arrests and weapons search
column6: High for the cable’s reported statement; actual arrests, weapons locations and operational scope remain unverified.
column7: FRUS d154 paragraph 3; unnamed contact.
column8: Compare Army and police arrest lists, seizure records, local orders and PKI/paramilitary records.

column2: The aide said Antara would be allowed to continue its anti-NEKOLIM line, but at a lower volume; the cable records an interlocutor’s report, not an independently checked press order or newsroom policy.
column4: Attributed report about news-agency policy and information control
column6: High for the reported statement; implementation and editorial changes require Antara records and dated content comparison.
column7: FRUS d154 paragraph 4.
column8: Compare Antara editions, editor/staff arrests, newsroom instructions and Army press directives.

column2: The Nasution aide said he had heard about Green’s approach to Indonesian official Suwito concerning detained missionary Harold Lovestrand and thought the approach could work. The FRUS note says Lovestrand had been held since August 1964, his wife and children were released in March 1965, and he was released on March 23, 1966 after U.S. representations.
column4: Personal/diplomatic channel and a detained foreign civilian, as reported by FRUS
column6: High for the published note’s account; the precise contacts, terms, reason for release and Indonesian file are not shown here.
column7: FRUS d154 paragraph 5 and footnote 4; cited Embtel 991 and March 1966 cable are not opened.
column8: Find Embassy consular case files, Suwito meeting notes, Indonesian detention register and the release cable; distinguish humanitarian representation from political bargaining.

column2: On 17 October Green assessed Sukarno and the Army as two rival but interdependent centers of power, each needing the other while trying to weaken the other; this is an Embassy model of the crisis, not an independently measured balance of authority.
column6: High for Green’s written assessment; actual command over ministries, provinces and armed units needs Indonesian records.
column7: FRUS d156 paragraph 2.A.
column8: Compare Presidential, Army, cabinet and regional command orders, appointments and implementation.

column2: Green reported that attacks on PKI installations had spread from Jakarta, with central Java under Army control in his account and sustained Communist–non-Communist confrontation in east Java and north Sumatra; he warned of possible escalation but did not provide a local incident list.
column4: Contemporary diplomatic reporting and regional risk assessment
column6: High that Green reported these conditions; low for regional representativeness and attribution without local records.
column7: FRUS d156 paragraph 2.C; Embassy analysis refers to observers and unnamed reports.
column8: Compare province and district incident chronologies, police logs, press, Army orders and named witness records.

column2: Green said different versions of the Army’s five demands to Sukarno circulated, with common elements reported as Suharto’s appointment to lead the Army, legal punishment of September 30 participants, reorganization of the Air Force, banning organizations or parties that supported the movement, and replacement of the PKI and Subandrio’s intelligence organization.
column4: Contemporary diplomatic report of reported Army demands
column6: High for the list Green summarized; moderate for whether it was an authoritative Army platform because the cable notes multiple versions.
column7: FRUS d156 paragraph 3.B.
column8: Find the original Army memorandum or Nasution/Suharto statement and compare Sukarno’s dated responses.

column2: Green reported that by 17 October Sukarno had appointed Suharto to head the Army and agreed to send Air Force chief Omar Dhani abroad, but had not yet named a regular replacement; Green said the Army was proceeding on its own to punish people it considered involved in September 30.
column4: Contemporary Embassy report on presidential concessions and Army actions
column6: High for what the Ambassador reported; appointment/departure dates, legal process and actual punishment require Indonesian decrees and case records.
column7: FRUS d156 paragraph 3.C.
column8: Check presidential decrees, Air Force personnel orders, court and detention files, and local execution records.

column2: Green forecast that press and National Front activity would remain contested between Sukarno and Army-aligned forces; he reported the Army remained dissatisfied with Antara and was interrogating and harassing its staff.
column4: Contemporary report and forecast about media control
column6: High for Green’s report and prediction; staff identities, legal basis, article changes and nationwide scope are not established.
column7: FRUS d156 paragraphs 5–6.
column8: Examine Antara archives, staff detention records, newsroom directives, newspaper closure orders and National Front minutes.

column2: Green speculated that Sukarno might seek a “new” or “indigenous” Communist party, while the Army preferred a total PKI ban and might instead press for a single party or National Front with a strong functional-group role; these are projected bargaining positions, not a formed party agreement.
column4: Contemporary policy forecast of party-system alternatives
column6: High that the cable described these possibilities; no outcome should be inferred from this forecast.
column7: FRUS d156 paragraphs 4 and 7.
column8: Compare subsequent presidential speeches, Army statements, party bans and National Front reorganization orders.

column2: Green’s d156 cable uses explicitly value-laden anti-Communist and religious language when interpreting Nasakom, Muslim political attitudes and relations with China; it is evidence of the Ambassador’s analytical frame, not a representative account of Muslim Indonesians or a neutral description of Nasakom.
column6: High for the language in the cable; it cannot establish Indonesian religious opinion or the causal effect of the Embassy’s framing.
column7: FRUS d156 paragraphs 2.D–E.
column8: Compare Indonesian Muslim organizations’ own statements, local publications and dissenting U.S. diplomatic analyses.

column2: On 20 October Green reported that the PKI had suffered major damage to its image, communications and command structure and some organizational damage from arrest, harassment and reported executions; he relayed estimates of roughly one thousand cadres arrested in Jakarta and several hundred executed.
column4: Contemporary U.S. Embassy report of state repression and estimated casualties
column6: High that the Embassy reported these estimates; the counts are unverified, one source line is withheld and no names or case register are supplied.
column7: FRUS d158 paragraphs 2–4; the cable uses “reportedly” for the arrest/execution counts and describes some evidence as direct but redacted.
column8: Obtain underlying Embassy source, Army/police rolls, prison registers, court and death records, and local victim lists.

column2: Green judged that the PKI’s basic organizational potential might recover if the party were again recognized and Army attacks stopped, while arguing that lasting suppression would require an attack on communism as an ideology and associated organizations; he praised the Army’s determination to destroy the PKI.
column4: Contemporary U.S. ambassadorial estimate and political preference
column6: High for the stated assessment and preference; it does not measure PKI capacity or establish the consequences of alternative policies.
column7: FRUS d158 paragraphs 4–6.
column8: Compare PKI membership and regional organization records with subsequent bans, arrests, labour and village-level association restrictions.

column2: In a 22 October memorandum to Johnson, McGeorge Bundy called events a “striking vindication” of U.S. policy since 1963 and the Bunker recommendations, described the Army as courageous and public support as extraordinary, and listed major unknowns including Sukarno’s health and role and Aidit’s whereabouts.
column6: High for Bundy’s written view; the claim about broad public support was not based on a survey in this memo, and “vindication” is an institutional judgment, not proof of U.S. causal control.
column7: FRUS d160, Indonesia section.
column8: Compare Johnson/Bundy decision records, earlier policy reviews, Indonesian public opinion evidence and internal dissent.

column2: In a 29 October tentative analysis, State treated Nasution’s 25 October speech and the public campaign against Subandrio as evidence that Army leaders intended an all-out fight against the PKI despite Sukarno’s opposition.
column4: Contemporary U.S. policy analysis based on attributed political signals
column6: High for the Department’s stated assessment; Nasution’s aims and Sukarno’s opposition need the underlying speeches and Indonesian records.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraphs 1–2.
column8: Read Nasution’s speech, Subandrio campaign materials, Sukarno’s dated response and Army operational orders.

column2: State assessed that Army leaders were trying to separate Sukarno from anti-Army advisers, isolate him and retain the option of using or removing him; this is the Department’s interpretation of Army strategy, not an Army order or proof of an agreed plan.
column4: U.S. policy analysis of Army–Presidential power struggle
column6: High for what the Department wrote; low as independent evidence of the Army’s internal decision-making.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraph 3.
column8: Compare Army leadership meeting records, Sukarno–Nasution communications and later command instructions.

column2: State predicted that the Army would increasingly act as Indonesia’s de facto government and might need to form a military or civil–military provisional government because it saw no other organized force able to lead after Nasakom’s collapse; this was a forecast and policy analysis.
column4: Contemporary U.S. forecast of succession and government formation
column6: High for the forecast’s text; it does not establish that the Army had already decided to seize formal governing power.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraphs 4–5.
column8: Compare October–December presidential, cabinet, Army and KOTI orders and provincial responses.

column2: State described the PKI as retreating amid “mass attacks encouraged by the Army” and forecast possible strikes, sabotage or guerrilla action; the Department’s expectation does not establish that PKI leadership had ordered such a response or that the attacks were centrally directed.
column4: Contemporary intelligence/policy scenario and attributed description
column6: High for the wording and scenario in the Department paper; operational attribution and local events remain unverified.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraph 4.
column8: Check Embassy situation reports, PKI orders, regional security files and local incident records.

column2: State advised that if Army leaders sought U.S. views, Washington should encourage a civil–military coalition rather than a military junta or purely civilian government; it saw long-standing U.S.–Indonesian Army service ties as an influence channel.
column4: U.S. political strategy recommendation and influence channel
column6: High for the proposed guidance; no evidence in this document that the Army asked for, received or followed the advice.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraphs 7–8.
column8: Find follow-up instructions, Army Attaché contacts, message receipts and Indonesian government negotiations.

column2: State proposed that food could be supplied through the International Red Cross if direct U.S. or other outside help embarrassed Army leaders; it listed Japan, Brazil, Malaysia, Thailand, Taiwan and South Korea as possible rice suppliers.
column6: High for the proposed channel and listed countries; no shipment, funding or Indonesian receipt is shown.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraph 8.d.
column8: Trace Red Cross discussions, donor-country decisions, rice purchase and shipping documents, and Indonesian receipt records.

column2: State proposed expert advice and possible IMF/partner assistance for Indonesia’s currency and credit crisis, while linking this option to a change in Indonesia’s recent attitude toward the IMF and other potential partners.
column4: Contingent international financial and policy channel
column6: High for the Department’s proposal and conditional framing; no IMF agreement or disbursement is established.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraph 8.e.
column8: Compare IMF Board records, Indonesian Finance Ministry requests, donor meeting notes and subsequent credit transfers.

column2: State said small arms and equipment might be needed if Army operations against the PKI expanded and proposed preparing for that contingency; this was not an arms authorization, purchase or delivery.
column6: High for the proposal; no specific model, quantity, recipient, funding or approved logistics route is given.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraph 8.f; later planning is separately documented in d164/C1232.
column8: Trace d164 onward, arms stock checks, third-country procurement, shipping, recipient lists and serial-number records.

column2: State considered using petroleum requirements to propose a de facto pause in nationalization of U.S. oil interests, so oil companies could provide full support to the Army and Indonesian economy; the document records an idea, not an agreed moratorium or company action.
column4: Economic leverage and private-company support proposal
column6: High for the proposal; no corporate decision, oil supply contract or policy adoption is shown.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraph 8.h.
column8: Compare State/Commerce oil policy, Caltex and Stanvac files, Indonesian nationalization instruments and company supply records.

column2: State expected the Army might first seek Japanese support and recommended quiet U.S.–Japanese consultations, with later consultation with Britain, Australia and others; Japanese aid, coordination and influence were still proposals.
column4: Third-country diplomatic coordination and aid-channel proposal
column6: High for the Department’s stated expectation and recommendation; no agreement or completed aid program is established by d163.
column7: FRUS d163 paragraphs 9–10; d164/C1232 records a subsequent interagency discussion, not an executed transfer.
column8: Obtain Japanese MOFA/Prime Minister records, London/Canberra responses, donor instruments and shipment/receipt records.

column2: The FRUS editorial note to d163 says the Jakarta Embassy on 2 November agreed with the broad analysis but emphasized that the Sukarno–Army contest remained unsettled, the Army still needed Sukarno and some leaders revered him, and the Embassy expected a long political struggle.
column4: Later Embassy reaction reported by an official editorial note
column6: High for what the FRUS editor reports; the cited November 2 telegram 1304 is not reproduced or independently opened.
column7: FRUS d163 editorial note 2, citing telegram 1304 from Djakarta.
column8: Open telegram 1304 and compare with subsequent presidential and Army decisions.

column2: Airgram A-398 separates two enclosures: an unclassified list of PKI leadership bodies as they stood after the May 1965 plenary, and a Secret, fragmentary report on leaders’ whereabouts explicitly based on limited information.
column4: Contemporary source scope, classification and information-quality statement
column6: High for the wording and markings on the scanned original; the document does not establish that the status enclosure was complete.
column7: A-398 original scan, cover and digital pp.1–6; enclosure 1 on pp.2–4 is marked unclassified; enclosure 2 on pp.5–6 is marked Secret. FRUS d185 summarizes its limited-information caveat.
column8: Compare the enclosure copies sent to State/other posts with any sanitized Indonesian copy; request original A-74 and attachments.

column2: A-398 warned that Embassy reports of prominent PKI leaders’ arrests often rested on suspect evidence and that alleged confessions were widely falsified; it cited an alleged Njono confession that seemed unaware of changes to the Politburo made at the May 1965 plenary.
column4: Contemporary Embassy assessment of evidence quality
column6: High that the Embassy made this assessment; whether each particular confession was fabricated is not independently resolved by A-398.
column7: A-398 original scan, digital p.1, paragraph 1; FRUS d185 editorial note, paragraph 2. This is a warning about the evidence available to the Embassy, not independent proof about Njono’s interrogation or the authenticity of every confession.
column8: Find the alleged Njono confession and compare its text with the May 1965 Politburo roster, interrogation records and independent custody evidence.

column2: In a June 1990 letter, Robert J. Martens acknowledged passing names of PKI leaders and senior cadres to non-Communist forces; he said the material came entirely from Indonesian Communist publications, covered at most a few thousand senior officials rather than rank and file, and that he acted without seeking or receiving Embassy permission.
column4: Retrospective first-person account of information source, transfer and authorization
column6: High that Martens publicly made this account; its accuracy about the full list, total number, authorization chain and recipients is not independently established by the letter.
column7: Martens, Washington Post letter to the editor, archived June 1/2, 1990; FRUS d185 reproduces the letter. Distinguish Martens’s account from Green’s 1966 A-74 report of a sanitized A-398 version made available to the Indonesian Government.
column8: Compare with the complete interview transcripts/tapes, list copies, contemporaneous Embassy clearance records and recipient registers.

column2: In a 1991 oral-history interview, Martens recalled that a chief aide to Adam Malik visited his house a few weeks after September 30 and asked for help; Martens says he passed basic material assembled from the Communist press to the aide, who took it to Malik, who “apparently” gave it to the Army, while Martens said he did not know what effect it had.
column4: Retrospective oral testimony about a possible interpersonal information-transfer route
column6: High for the content of Martens’s published recollection; low for exact timing, identity/receipt at each later link, whether this was the same sanitized A-398 copy, and any operational effect.
column7: ADST excerpt from Martens oral history, paragraphs shown under “I had assembled all this unclassified data” (2016 web edition); the interview itself uses approximate language and the full tape/transcript was not compared.
column8: Read the complete ADST transcript and Kadane’s deposited recordings/transcripts; identify the aide from independent Indonesian sources and locate Malik/Army receipt records.

column2: A July 1990 New York Times report said interviewees did not dispute that names were passed to Indonesians, but found disagreement over whether Martens acted alone or senior Embassy/CIA officials coordinated the transfer and over the list’s importance; excerpts of Kadane’s recorded interviews appeared ambiguous on some officials’ advance knowledge or approval.
column4: Contemporary journalistic account of a disputed retrospective investigation
column6: High for what the published article reported; the article is not a substitute for the underlying tapes, transcripts, transfer records or Indonesian files and does not settle the dispute.
column7: Michael Wines, “C.I.A. Tie Asserted in Indonesia Purge,” New York Times, 12 July 1990, full text through an Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network reprint, lines 17–50; compare Kadane’s May 21 report and Martens’s June letter.
column8: Retrieve the reporter’s full source transcripts, Kadane’s original recordings and complete Green/Lydman/Masters interviews; compare each exact question and response.

column2: GerakIngatan catalogs a 1978 Komitee Indonesië congress titled Het Andere Indonesia about development aid and the perspective of ordinary Indonesians; the catalog cites IISH solidarity-movement collection COLL00284.
column6: High for catalog existence and description; no verified congress proceedings or actual participants.
column7: GerakIngatan item KOL4_26 catalog directly opened; descriptive statement is curatorial metadata rather than independently read congress records.
column8: Retrieve permitted scan/proceedings; identify date, venue, participants, IGGI-related proposals and independently check implementation.

column2: GerakIngatan catalogs a 1987 obituary for Ernst Utrecht, attributed in its description to Suparna Sastra Diredja and published in Indonesia Feiten en Meningen; its creator metadata instead lists Utrecht family names.
column6: High for catalog wording; no confidence assigned to unexamined obituary contents.
column7: GerakIngatan KOL22_17 catalog opened; metadata author/creator discrepancy explicitly retained.
column8: Legally inspect image, check masthead and byline, compare with Utrecht personal archive and independent biography.

column2: In a retrospective first-person account Fridus Steijlen states that he joined Komitee Indonesië as a volunteer in 1978; Basuki Resobowo produced illustrations for its Indonesië Feiten en Meningen magazine and protest posters; Steijlen describes joint cultural work in Amsterdam around 1984.
column6: Moderate for participant recollection; requires contemporary corroboration
column7: Full GerakIngatan narrative read; distinguishes narrator testimony from independent proof of dates, circulation and demonstrator lists.
column8: Compare signed magazine issues and poster imprints with IISH COLL00284; establish event dates, roles and other witnesses.

column2: GerakIngatan catalog KOL15_11 identifies a photograph attributed to De Waarheid of 7 June 1985 page 1 depicting Suparna Sastra Diredja and Ernst Utrecht in a protest against IGGI-linked aid; original newspaper page remains unread.
column6: High for catalog metadata; provisional for photo identification
column7: Opened GerakIngatan full catalog; Delpher resolver link failed in web reader. Exact paper title and date given in source field.
column8: Open Delpher scan via alternative viewer or library; check photo caption, demonstration date and participant identities.

column2: In an April 10, 1997 letter, reporter Kathy Kadane said she had transferred her taped interviews, notes and a small group of documents, including some declassified cables, to the National Security Archive at George Washington University.
column4: Reporter’s statement about research records and archival provenance
column6: High that Kadane publicly made this statement; the deposit inventory and current physical or access status of each item are not independently verified.
column7: NYRB publisher-hosted exchange, Kadane letter, paragraph 2 (1997). This confirms a published statement, not that a particular tape or full transcript can now be located or accessed.
column8: Locate the National Security Archive accession, box/folder inventory, and access rules; identify recordings, notes, exhibits and any restrictions.

column2: In the 1997 NYRB letter, Kadane reported that the Pentagon supplied jeeps and that U.S. officials supplied “dozens” of field radios to Indonesian Army forces during the post-September 30 crisis; she separately attributed the Collins KWM-2 procurement to CIA in the next part of her account.
column4: Retrospective journalist-reported allegation of logistical supply
column6: High for what Kadane reported; low/unverified for the number, timing, recipient units, shipment and use because no itemized delivery record is attached or located.
column7: NYRB exchange, Kadane letter, paragraphs 4–5. The article distinguishes Pentagon jeeps, general U.S. radios, and an unnamed former Embassy official’s more specific CIA/Collins-radio account; it does not append a shipment manifest, receipt or operational log.
column8: Seek Pentagon/CIA procurement and surplus records, Clark Field inventory and flight logs, serial numbers, Kostrad and recipient-unit inventories, and Indonesian-side receipts.

column2: Kadane reported that an unnamed former Embassy official described CIA-provided Collins KWM-2 high-frequency radios held at Clark Field in the Philippines, secretly flown to Indonesia by the U.S. Air Force and delivered to Suharto’s Kostrad headquarters by Pentagon representatives.
column6: High that Kadane published this attributed account; low/unverified for model, number, staging location, flight, recipient and date because the source’s identity and supporting records are unavailable here.
column7: NYRB exchange, Kadane letter, paragraphs 5–6; source is an unnamed former official as presented in Kadane’s article. Do not merge with the distinct three Motorola P-31 radios in FRUS d155 or the later HF communications program in d175/d211.
column8: Find CIA logistics files, USAF C-130/Clark Field movement records, radio serial/inventory records, Kostrad receipts and the full interview and notes.

column2: Kadane said a former U.S. official described the CIA providing Indonesian Army radio frequencies to the National Security Agency in advance, an NSA site in Southeast Asia intercepting and translating the traffic, and resulting reporting being sent to Washington alongside Embassy reporting.
column6: High for the published allegation; low/unverified for the actual intercepts, location, tasking, translations, reporting chain and use because no NSA/CIA collection records or interview tape were examined.
column7: NYRB exchange, Kadane letter, paragraphs 6–7. FRUS d175 documents a proposed covert communications system and U.S. links but does not by itself prove NSA monitoring of that system.
column8: Search NSA/CIA declassified SIGINT and liaison files, frequency-allocation records, site logs, translation reports and the Kadane interview tape/transcript.

column2: Kadane reported that an unnamed former U.S. official said NSA intercepts included orders from Suharto’s intelligence unit to kill specific persons at specified locations.
column4: Retrospective journalist-reported allegation about target-specific lethal orders
column6: High that Kadane published this allegation; unverified as an actual intercept or order, with no Indonesian command record, victim identification, signal transcript or independent source located.
column7: NYRB exchange, Kadane letter, paragraph 7. Keep the alleged order, whether transmitted, whether received, whether acted upon and any resulting death as separate questions.
column8: Obtain the alleged intercept transcript and underlying NSA report; identify the unit/person/location only from original records; compare against Indonesian orders and independent victim/custody records.

column2: In the 1997 NYRB exchange, Robert L. Barry rejected the theory that Suharto and possibly the CIA conspired in the 1965 coup and aftermath, and argued that the ensuing violence was more readily explained as a spontaneous release of pent-up social tensions.
column6: High that Barry published this interpretation; it is not contemporaneous evidence of 1965 operations or a substitute for archival corroboration.
column7: NYRB exchange, Barry letter, paragraphs 7–9. Barry identifies himself there as U.S. Ambassador to Indonesia in 1992–1995, not as a 1965 witness.
column8: Assess the 1965 causal question from contemporary Indonesian, U.S., British, Australian, Dutch and other records, plus independent local histories; do not treat this letter as direct evidence.

column2: In her reply to Barry in the same 1997 exchange, Jeri Laber disputed his “spontaneous explosion” explanation, citing scholarly agreement about Army arming and inciting local attacks and asserting evidence of U.S. moral and financial support; she called for release of Indonesian and U.S. records.
column4: Later editor’s published interpretation and evidence claim
column6: High that Laber published this response; the scholarly sources and underlying financial records must be checked independently and are not established by the letter alone.
column7: NYRB exchange, Laber reply, paragraphs 10–13. Her statement records an interpretation and a pointer to other evidence, not a substitute for those sources.
column8: Trace her cited article and the primary evidence it references; compare with Indonesian Army orders, local organizational records, and independently documented U.S. finance.

column2: Bunnell states that his 1990 reconstruction relied primarily on U.S. government documents and interviews with more than 75 former American officials; he describes Jakarta dissertation research in 1963–65 and says his 1981–82 Indonesian-source work had very limited success.
column6: High that the article describes its method this way; the underlying interview set and notes are not available in this record.
column7: Bunnell, pp. 29 and note 5; full Cornell-hosted article sections read.
column8: Locate Bunnell’s interview notes and any deposited papers; identify which claims rely on Sukendro or the same former officials.

column2: Bunnell reports that General Sukendro confirmed in interviews in 1981–82 that the U.S. had secretly supplied medicines, radios and small arms through the CIA station in Bangkok.
column4: Retrospective recipient account reported by a historian
column6: High that Bunnell published this statement; medium for the reported interview content; actual delivery timing, quantities, radio types, recipients and weapon use remain unverified because the interview record is not open here.
column7: Bunnell, p. 60 and note 152; compare FRUS d171 (Nov. 5: no discussion of providing weapons or radios beyond approved medicine), d173 (Nov. 10 request), d175/d211 (distinct communications proposal and later stages). Do not treat other authors repeating Bunnell as independent confirmation.
column8: Find Bunnell’s Sukendro interview recording, notes or deposited papers; locate Bangkok station procurement, shipment and Army receipt/issue records, especially small-arms serials and recipient units.

column2: Bunnell concludes that the United States was not a prime instigator of the failed September 30 Movement or the massacres, but was an important and knowing accomplice to the Army-led campaign; he also cautions that the extent of CIA activity could not be finally judged without withheld records.
column4: Retrospective historian’s causal and political interpretation
column6: High that Bunnell states this conclusion; the causal interpretation remains the author’s analysis and must not be substituted for the user’s political judgment.
column7: Bunnell, pp. 30 and 60; he explicitly discusses incomplete/declassified records and uncertainty about the CIA station.
column8: Compare with later archival releases and differently argued scholarship; keep the full causal chain and the user’s judgment separate.

column2: In a 1987 interview Green said he personally ordered all fourteen emergency walkie-talkies held by the U.S. Embassy transferred to Suharto, without a request, to provide internal security and signal U.S. concern; in the preceding account he says his first private meeting with Suharto was May 29, 1966, but gives no exact handover date.
column3: Following the interview’s May 29, 1966 context; recalled 1987
column4: Retrospective first-person testimony about a separate Embassy equipment transfer
column6: High for what Green said; medium for the transfer as a firsthand but 21-year-later account; low for exact date/model/serial, signed receipt and effect. Do not merge with three P-31 sets discussed in the October 1965 telegram.
column7: ADST oral history, interviewer Robert J. Martens, transcript around pp. 25–27; compare FRUS d155, which records a separate three-set P-31 offer and planned Oct. 14 turnover.
column8: Find Green’s report and Bundy response cable, Embassy emergency radio inventory, issue/receipt records and Suharto security-office inventory.

column2: On Nov. 4, State authorized processing Sukendro’s medical-supply request but said it was handling a separately mentioned communications-equipment matter in the Jakarta–Washington channel and did not want it discussed with Sukendro; it also said not to pursue arms with him at that point. The wording about equipment “passed from Djakarta” is partly redacted.
column4: Contemporary U.S. policy instruction with redacted operational reference
column6: High for the unredacted instruction; low/unresolved for what equipment moved, sender/recipient, date and route because the phrase is redacted.
column7: FRUS d170, paragraphs 1–5; State says it is “looking separately” at the communications issue and limits contact with Sukendro.
column8: Request the full RG 59 telegram and referenced Jakarta 1333/State 749 cables; compare Embassy equipment logs and Army receipt records.

column2: The Nov. 5 Bangkok cable records that Sukendro designated an Army colonel to discuss small-arms needs and a police colonel to bring a communications-equipment list, but explicitly says there was no discussion of U.S. provision of weapons or communications gear beyond the medical aid already approved.
column4: Contemporary covert-liaison record and aid-stage distinction
column6: High for the cable’s wording and recorded meeting; it does not show whether requests were later approved or delivered.
column7: FRUS d171 paragraphs 1–5 and footnote 6; distinguish the forthcoming lists from an agreement to supply.
column8: Read the referenced missing cables and Nov. 6 guidance; find later decisions, Bangkok station procurement and Army acknowledgements.

column2: In a Nov. 10 Bangkok meeting report, Sukendro said senior Army leaders in Jakarta lacked portable voice radios and requested about a dozen sets for Nasution, Suharto, Umar, Sukendro and other senior officers, plus the Paracommandos and possibly a guard battalion.
column4: Contemporary U.S. cable reporting an Army communications request
column6: High that the U.S. cable records these named proposed users; the Army’s actual inventory and need are not independently verified by this report.
column7: FRUS d173 paragraphs 3–4. This is a requested system, distinct from d155 P-31 offer and the later 303 proposal.
column8: Find the original Sukendro request/list, Army communications inventory and any purchase or serial/receipt log.

column2: The same Nov. 11 cable records a separate request for a Jakarta-based voice circuit connecting Medan, Palembang, Bandung, Semarang, Surabaya, Makassar and Banjarmasin, possibly Yogyakarta, plus a Central Java tactical communications study; Sukendro described these as Army requirements and said the existing long-range voice net was lacking.
column6: High for the reported list and attributed assessment; actual network coverage, equipment loss and operational consequences require local records.
column7: FRUS d173 paragraphs 5–7; this was a second network concept separate from portable sets.
column8: Find Army signal corps plans, city-level radio inventories, frequencies, local command logs and Indonesian procurement/installation records.

column2: The Nov. 11 Embassy proposal said the Army lacked funds and, if Washington acceded, commercially available radios could be covertly procured and delivered through a transfer point whose text is redacted; Sukendro said the Army could receive and forward them. The Embassy estimated about $40,000 for a stock configuration with voice and CW capability.
column4: Contemporary covert procurement and logistics proposal
column6: High for the proposal and redacted route reference; it is conditional and does not establish approval, payment, shipment, receipt or operation.
column7: FRUS d173 paragraphs 8–9 and footnotes 6–7; the estimate is not a realized invoice.
column8: Obtain the missing follow-on telegram 952, the NARA RG 59 file, 303 minutes, purchase/freight documents, transfer-point records and recipient receipts.

column2: A FRUS editorial note to d173 reports that on Nov. 12 the Department told Australian, New Zealand and British Embassy officials that the U.S. had agreed to send $100,000 in medicines and was seriously considering $50,000 in commercial communications equipment; the cited underlying Telegram 373 was not reproduced in this source.
column4: Official editorial report of allied diplomatic notification
column6: High for what the published FRUS note reports; the original cable, allied reactions and actual medical/radio delivery remain unverified.
column7: FRUS d173 footnote 7; compare its $50,000 consideration with the Bangkok Embassy’s separate $40,000 stock-item estimate in paragraph 9.
column8: Retrieve Telegram 373 and U.S./Australian/New Zealand/British diplomatic files; trace the medical shipment and any communications contracts or dispatches.

column2: Brad Simpson’s 2010 essay states that covert U.S. assistance apparently included small arms delivered to the Indonesian Army through the CIA station in Bangkok; the publisher-hosted version read here supplies no inline note for that sentence.
column6: High that Simpson published the assertion; low as independent confirmation of delivery because the article’s local source trail is not shown and it may rely on the Bunnell/Sukendro interview or the same U.S. records.
column7: Inside Indonesia 99, paragraphs 27–36; compare Bunnell p. 60/note 152 and the explicit initial holds in d170/d171. Treat as historiography, not receipt evidence.
column8: Trace Simpson’s cited chapter/archive notes in Economists with Guns; seek declassified CIA station records and Indonesian Army weapons issue/receipt lists.

column2: FRUS d177 reports, through its note citing the Nov. 16 Embassy Airgram 331, that Sukarno told the Cabinet on Nov. 6 that former Ambassador Howard Jones had given an unnamed Indonesian Rp150 million to spread “Free World” ideology. This establishes that Green’s cable recorded the allegation, not that Jones made a payment.
column4: Contemporary U.S. record of a reported Indonesian presidential accusation
column6: High that the U.S. cable reports the accusation; unverified whether any payment occurred, who the unnamed recipient was, or what the funds were for.
column7: FRUS d177 footnote 3 points to Embassy Airgram 331, Nov. 16, POL 2-1 INDON; neither the speech transcript nor underlying airgram was opened. The footnote is not an accounting record.
column8: Retrieve Airgram 331 and the Nov. 6 Cabinet speech/Indonesian press reports; identify the named recipient only from primary evidence; trace any U.S. appropriations, disbursement or covert-action accounts and compare competing U.S./Indonesian accounts.

column2: In a printed excerpt of Kathy Kadane’s December 1989 interview with Edward Masters, Masters assents to the account that Martens and others compiled PKI biographical index cards in an interagency team in the Embassy political section, that CIA material was cross-indexed with other information, and that PKI names were circulated among Embassy officials for their own additions.
column4: Selected retrospective oral-history testimony about data collection and interagency handling
column6: High that the published excerpt prints Masters’s assent; medium that it captures the full interview context or complete process, because the audio and unabridged transcript were not heard/read.
column7: CovertAction Information Bulletin no. 35, p. 59, section “The Indonesia Transcripts”; the interview is attributed to Dec. 1989. Kadane’s prompts supply some of the description; Masters’s replies are brief. The excerpt gives no index-card files, names, handling logs, dates, scope of CIA inputs or use by Indonesian recipients.
column8: Locate the original Kadane audio/transcript and notes at the National Security Archive; seek Martens’s card files, Embassy circulation records, CIA cross-index entries and transfer/receipt documentation; compare against FRUS d185/A-74 and Indonesian list copies.

column2: In a May 14, 1990 interview excerpt, Jack Lydman agreed that senior Embassy officials cooperated in supervising/checking names, acknowledged that names of arrested or killed people were reported back from Suharto’s headquarters, but said he did not remember the exact sequence and could not identify the principal U.S. contact with Ali Murtopo.
column4: Selected retrospective testimony on Embassy oversight and feedback reporting
column6: High that the printed excerpt contains these statements; medium for the underlying chain and its completeness, given the selected excerpt and lack of audio.
column7: CovertAction Information Bulletin no. 35, pp. 58–59. The excerpt simultaneously supports senior-level cooperation and records Lydman’s uncertainty about the precise return chain/contact; neither should be dropped when summarizing it.
column8: Obtain full audio/transcript and Kadane’s notes; compare Green, Masters, Tovar, Ethel and Martens accounts with Embassy reporting, Martens list files, Ali Murtopo/Suharto headquarters records and any returned-name logs.

column2: In a Dec. 20, 1989 excerpt, Kadane told Marshall Green that Masters had identified a group decision for Martens to disseminate names to an Army emissary, listing Green, CIA station chief Hugh Tovar, Masters, Defense Attaché Willis Ethel and Lydman; Green’s printed response is “Yeah.”
column4: Selected retrospective testimony attributed to the Ambassador about authorization
column6: High that the excerpt prints this question, list and response; medium for its precise meaning because the interviewer supplies the group description and the full question/answer context is unavailable.
column7: CovertAction Information Bulletin no. 35, p. 59. The brief affirmation does not establish the date, exact material, number of names, recipient identity, written authorization, intended use, subsequent transfer or effect.
column8: Hear the complete Dec. 20 Green recording and read Kadane’s transcript/notes; locate Embassy/303/State approval or distribution records, Martens list copies, and Army intermediary receipts.
